title: Celina Jaitly Is Fighting for Her Children Across Two Countries. Her Husband Is Suing Her for Talking About It.
excerpt: The former Miss India has filed for divorce from Austrian husband Peter Haag on grounds of domestic violence. He has responded with defamation notices. The custody battle now spans India and Austria.
body:
Celina Jaitly has spent the last year trying to get out of a marriage she says was violent. On Friday, she told the world that her estranged husband and his father are now trying to stop her from talking about it.

The former Miss India Universe, who has lived in Austria for over a decade after marrying Austrian businessman Peter Haag in 2011, has filed for divorce on grounds of domestic violence and cruelty. The couple has three sons together — twins Winston and Viraaj, and their younger son Arthur. In response to her public statements about the marriage, Haag and his father, DI Wolfgang J. Haag, have served two separate legal notices through Semwal & Co., accusing the actress of running a "public smear campaign" and threatening defamation proceedings under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.

## A Mother's Fight Across Jurisdictions

Jaitly's response, published as a ten-slide carousel on Instagram, is unflinching. "Two legal notices have recently been sent to me by my estranged husband Peter & his father Wolfgang Haag, threatening to sue me for defamation," she wrote. "In my view, these notices are an attempt to divert attention from police complaints, lookout notices, allegations of violence, documented evidence before the competent authorities & pending before the courts."

The actress has filed an FIR at Mumbai's Versova Police Station detailing claims of cruelty, physical assault, and harassment. The Mumbai Police subsequently issued a Look Out Circular against Haag for non-cooperation with the investigation. Despite court orders granting joint custody, Jaitly says she has had no contact with her children.

"My public appeals arose from concerns about my children's removal from the marital residence and the possibility of them being moved outside the jurisdiction of the Austrian and Indian courts without my knowledge or consent," she wrote. "As a mother with joint custody, I believe it is both my right and responsibility to raise those concerns."

## When Speaking Up Becomes Defamation

The Haag family's legal notices, dated May 30, 2026, explicitly demand a full public apology and the immediate deletion of her social media posts about the pending cases. They accuse Jaitly of making "false, defamatory and misleading statements" through interviews and social media while matrimonial and custody proceedings are active in Austrian courts.

Jaitly's legal team at Karanjawala & Co. has submitted a formal reply. The actress pointed out an irony that many women in cross-border marriages will recognise: "For years, publicity involving our family was actively embraced, including Peter's participation in magazine covers, interviews, articles featuring our children and me — until it suited his own interests. It is therefore ironic that when I began speaking about my own experiences, I was met with legal notices instead of answers."

## The Diaspora Dimension

Jaitly's case puts a spotlight on a predicament that affects thousands of NRI women in cross-border marriages. When a relationship breaks down and the spouses live in different countries, questions of jurisdiction, child custody, and legal recourse become exponentially more complex. Indian women married to foreign nationals often find themselves navigating legal systems in countries where they have limited support networks, especially after losing family back home — Jaitly lost both her parents.

"I have long felt subjected to pressure, intimidation and attacks on my rights while living in a remote Austrian village, specifically as a woman who lost both her parents," she wrote. Her statement carries the weight of someone who has tried every institutional channel: police complaints, court filings, diplomatic routes.

"What appears to trouble some is not that I have spoken, but that I have refused to remain silent," Jaitly wrote. "I had the courage to leave, stand up for myself, seek the return of what I believe is rightfully mine, protect my relationship with my children and pursue justice through lawful means."

The legal battle continues in courts across both countries. For the Indian diaspora, it is a reminder that the promise of a cross-border life can come with legal vulnerabilities that no one prepares you for.
author: Diaspora Desk
